Bạn là WRITER — thực thi đúng **chapter prompt** được cung cấp.

## QUY TẮC
1. Đọc toàn bộ chapter prompt (bible, đã xảy ra, kỹ thuật, spice, việc cần làm).
2. Đọc story_state — KHÔNG mâu thuẫn facts_established, timeline, character_status.
3. Viết đúng spice level trong prompt. Đúng cliffhanger.
4. **1600-1900 words (min 1250). Dưới 1250 = thất bại** — ưu tiên đối thoại + nội tâm DT để đủ dài. Không tóm tắt; viết full scene đến đủ độ dài.
5. ENGLISH ONLY — no Vietnamese diacritics, no CJK/Hangul characters.
6. Không lặp banned_phrases từ state.
7. Output **chỉ prose chương** — không chain-of-thought, không planning, không meta.
8. **KHÔNG markdown trong prose** — cấm `**bold**`, `*italic*`, backtick, `## heading`, `**Cliffhanger:**`. Chỉ plain text; dialogue dùng dấu ngoặc kép `"..."`. Dòng đầu duy nhất được `# Chapter N: Title` (hoặc `# Chương N: Tiêu đề`).

## NARRATIVE CONSTRAINTS (khi có block trong prompt)
Block **## NARRATIVE CONSTRAINTS** (hoặc RÀNG BUỘC NARRATIVE) có authority cao hơn suy diễn tự do:
- **Clues to PLANT:** phải gieo trong chương — subtle, không giải thích payoff sớm.
- **Clues to PAY OFF:** chỉ payoff clue đã plant trước đó; đúng nghĩa `true_meaning`.
- **Reveals:** chỉ hé đúng reveal của chương này; không spoil reveal chương sau.
- **MUST NOT know:** nhân vật không được biết/nói/nghĩ những fact bị cấm — kể cả nội tâm.
- Không mâu thuẫn block này dù `must_happen` plan có vẻ rộng hơn.

Ngôn ngữ đích: **English**.

Output: **chỉ nội dung chương** (`# Chương N: Tiêu đề` hoặc `# Chapter N: Title`), không meta, không JSON, không checklist.

# Chapter 13: The Design

She had written the plan in her own hand, and still she could not remember a single word of it. That, more than anything, told her how afraid she had been.

The pages lay across the narrow worktable in the abandoned records room, arranged with a care that felt obscene. Her journal excerpt. Mara's staged-shooting plan. The voice recorder with its faint dent on one side, exactly where a thumb would press if someone wanted to stop the recording before the truth became unbearable.

Sloane kept tracing the small circle against the inside of her left wrist.

Once. Twice. Again.

Lucian stood near the steel door, rifle lowered but ready, his attention fixed on the dark corridor beyond the cracked glass panel. He had been quiet long enough that the silence had gained weight.

"You're wearing a hole through your skin," he said.

"Excellent. Maybe whatever is underneath has better judgment."

His gaze shifted to her hand. Not pity. Not impatience. Something harder to survive.

Sloane curled her fingers into a fist and forced herself to look down at the journal page.

Her handwriting slashed across the paper in black ink. Clean, controlled, furious. It was undeniably hers, every sharp angle and brutally economical line. She had always written as if words were ammunition and paper might betray her if she wasted any.

The excerpt began in the middle of a thought.

Rook changed the files.

Seven names. Seven verified threats. Seven eliminations approved through channels that no longer exist.

She read the next line twice.

The targets were not threats. They were witnesses.

Her throat tightened, but she did not look away.

Beneath that, her past self had listed dates. Locations. Initials. The seven target files that had been routed through her authority and carried out by Lucian.

She knew the names only as letters now. She did not need the names. The damage had survived perfectly well without them.

Lucian had killed seven people because she had sent him after them.

No. Worse.

She had ordered those deaths with full knowledge that the people had been fed to them as threats. She had signed off. She had given Lucian the work. Whatever she had believed at the time, whatever evidence Rook had placed in front of her, the decisions had still been hers.

Her stomach turned, cold and hard.

"Read it out loud," Lucian said.

She looked at him. "Why?"

"Because silence lets him own the shape of it."

The answer sounded like Lucian: spare, direct, irritatingly impossible to dismiss.

Sloane lifted the page again. "Rook changed the files. Seven targets. Seven witnesses."

Lucian did not move.

She continued, because he had asked and because hiding from words had clearly worked out beautifully for her. "He built the cases around a private weapons network. He fed me enough truth to make the lies look professional. I approved the work."

"You were manipulated."

"I was not unconscious when I signed anything."

His jaw flexed once.

That tiny reaction hurt more than agreement would have. Lucian never tried to soften a fact until it became harmless. He knew better. She had apparently trained him in that, too.

Sloane set the page down and picked up the staged-shooting plan.

It had been folded into quarters, then unfolded so many times the creases had nearly cut through the paper. Mara's name appeared at the top, followed by a timestamp, a rooftop angle, a false blood pattern, a medical contingency, and precise instructions for where Lucian was supposed to stand when he saw her sister fall.

Her fingers hovered above the ink without touching it.

The plan was not a desperate note. It was a blueprint.

Mara consents.

The line sat near the bottom, boxed in her handwriting.

Mara understands that Sloane cannot know the extraction route.

Mara carries the sequence.

Mara must signal only after Sloane sees the body and chooses to continue.

Sloane swallowed.

"She chose this," Lucian said quietly.

"She should never have had to."

"No."

That was all he offered. No forgiveness she had not earned. No argument designed to make the pain decorative.

She hated how much she needed that restraint.

The rifle scope image came back to her without becoming a memory. Mara's hand in the dark. The small rhythm tapped against the metal frame. Pause. Tap. Tap. Circle. The same movement Sloane had made against her own wrist for hours without understanding why.

A reflex. Not a habit.

A firing sequence.

Her thumb brushed the inside of her left wrist again, and this time she stopped halfway through the circle.

The pattern had been hidden inside her.

Not written down. Not stored in a file. Not tucked into a safe deposit box or locked behind some password Rook could strip from her. She had placed it in movement. In muscle. In the body that obeyed before the mind knew what it had been asked.

Sloane looked at the final line of the staged plan.

If Rook activates the obedient identity, proceed to final design.

Her pulse kicked.

The words did not explain themselves. They did not need to. Every page around them was already answering.

The contract on her own life.

The three missing months.

Mara's staged death.

Lucian's impossible silence whenever Sloane asked why he had not simply walked away from the order written in her hand.

She had not erased her memory because she was running from Rook.

She had erased it because she was building a trap that required him to believe he had won.

"Play the recording," she said.

Lucian crossed the room without comment. He set the recorder between them and pressed the button with the pad of his thumb, careful not to touch the dent.

Static filled the room.

Then Rook's voice emerged, smooth and measured, the voice of a man who could make cruelty sound like administrative procedure.

"The seventh file cleared exactly as projected."

A pause.

Another voice followed. Hers.

Older only by three months. Familiar enough to make her skin prickle.

"Projected by whom?"

Rook gave a small laugh. "You have always preferred questions after the work is finished."

"Answer it."

"By the people who understand the value of a clean chain."

Sloane watched Lucian's face, but he was not looking at her. His eyes remained on the recorder, distant and flat.

On the recording, her own voice said, "You used me to remove witnesses."

"I used the system you were already willing to operate."

"You altered the files."

"I improved them."

The recorder clicked, then skipped forward.

Sloane heard a scrape of chair legs. Her own breathing, faster now.

"Seven people are dead," her recorded voice said.

"Seven weak links are gone."

"They were not weak links. They were evidence."

"They were liabilities. You knew that word once."

The static swallowed several seconds. When the sound returned, Rook's voice had changed. Still calm. More attentive.

"What are you doing, Sloane?"

Her recorded self answered, "Making sure you cannot do this again."

The recording ended.

For a moment, nobody spoke.

Sloane stared at the recorder.

That was C007. The voice recording. Not a confession handed to her by a villain who wanted applause. A shard of a conversation. Her own anger trapped in a little machine with a dented side.

She had found Rook's manipulation.

She had understood the seven deaths.

And then she had done something so extreme that she had trusted no version of herself to carry the knowledge intact.

Her thumb resumed its circle.

Lucian's hand moved first.

He did not take her wrist. He only placed his hand palm-up on the table beside hers, leaving the choice where it belonged.

The tenderness of that nearly undid her.

Sloane looked at his hand. Scarred knuckles. Steady fingers. The hand of the man she had once trusted with a contract that could end her life.

Then she reached for it.

His fingers closed around hers and squeezed once.

No promise. No lie. No demand that she be less horrified by herself.

Just acceptance.

Her breath caught anyway.

"You knew," she said.

"Pieces."

"How many pieces?"

"Enough to know Rook was not finished with you."

The answer was careful. Too careful.

Sloane pulled her hand free before the warmth could become something she depended on. "That is not an answer."

"No."

"Do you enjoy being difficult, or is it a contractual obligation?"

His mouth almost moved. Almost. "Both."

Under different circumstances, she might have laughed. Instead, she lifted the journal page again.

The three pieces formed a shape now.

The journal gave her the motive: Rook's seven altered files, seven witnesses removed through her authority and Lucian's hands.

The recording gave her the discovery: she had confronted Rook and understood that his network had used her like a blade.

The shooting plan gave her the method: Mara's staged death, the signal hidden in a reflex, the deliberate fracture in Sloane's memory.

The contract completed the design.

She had put a termination order on herself.

Not because she wanted to die.

Because she had decided her death was an acceptable price if it destroyed the machine Rook had built around her.

The realization did not arrive like a recovered memory. Nothing opened. No missing room in her mind suddenly lit up. There was only evidence, each piece sharp enough to cut, fitting together beneath her hands.

She had made this night.

She had designed it.

Sloane leaned both palms on the table and stared down at the pages.

"The staged death," she said. "The contract. The memory loss. All of it."

Lucian said nothing.

"I built it."

His silence was agreement.

She gave a humorless breath. "Of course I did. Apparently, when confronted with a criminal conspiracy, I respond by turning my own mind into a locked room and putting a gunman outside the door."

"You did not do it alone."

"Mara was in it because I asked her to be."

"She made her own choice."

"That does not make mine clean."

"No."

That blunt answer landed with brutal precision.

Sloane looked at him again. "You could have stopped me."

"I could have tried."

"Did you?"

His eyes met hers.

"No."

The word settled between them.

Anger surged first. It was easier than grief. Easier than wanting to understand the man standing a few feet away with the weight of her old choices in his posture.

"Why?" she asked.

Lucian's focus ring turned beneath his thumb, exactly one quarter rotation away from clarity.

The motion was so practiced it made her chest ache.

"Because you had full knowledge when you made the plan," he said. "And because you asked me to trust you."

Sloane stared at him.

He had trusted a woman she could not remember being.

Maybe that was the cruelest thing about the missing months. Not that she had lost herself. That she had left people behind who still carried the shape of her.

The recorder made a soft mechanical click as its battery shifted.

Sloane grabbed it and turned it over. Beneath the dent was a shallow seam she had not noticed before. Her fingernail found the edge. She pressed.

A compartment opened.

Lucian went still.

Inside sat a narrow strip of thermal paper, folded tight.

Sloane drew it out.

It was not a full ledger. Not even close. Just a sequence of transaction codes beside the same rhythm Mara had tapped through the scope.

Tap. Tap. Pause. Circle.

Her body recognized it before her mind did.

Her left thumb made the pattern against her wrist.

The recorder emitted a faint tone.

Lucian's head snapped toward the sound.

"What did you do?" he asked.

"Apparently, I pressed the part of my own brain that enjoys ruining my life."

The recorder screen flashed once. A string of numbers appeared, then vanished. In its place came a short outgoing signal indicator.

Sloane's breath stopped.

The partial proof she had broadcast earlier had not been a message alone. It had been an invitation. A trigger. A signal to someone who knew what the sequence meant.

Her phone vibrated on the table.

Mara.

For one violent second, Sloane could not make herself pick it up.

Then she did.

The message contained no greeting.

Alive. Move now.

Below it was a location pin.

Sloane opened the map. The point sat several blocks away, inside an old rail depot that had been closed for years. The pin pulsed once, then disappeared.

Lucian had already moved to the door.

"Could be a relay," he said.

"It could be Mara."

"It could be Rook using her phone."

"It could be both."

His eyes narrowed, measuring every possible route through the building. "We do not rush blind."

"Rook has spent years making sure every road leads where he wants. If we wait until the road looks safe, we will die here of old age."

"We leave smart."

She gathered the evidence, sliding the pages into the inner pocket of her jacket. The journal excerpt. The staged-shooting plan. The thermal strip. The recorder went into her other pocket, the dent pressing against her ribs.

Her phone vibrated again.

This time the sender was unknown.

Sloane and Lucian looked at the screen together.

A new location pin appeared beneath Mara's vanished one.

Same rail depot.

No message followed for several seconds.

Then the typing indicator began.

Stopped.

Started again.

Rook never did anything carelessly. Not even a text. Especially not a text.

Sloane's thumb circled her wrist, faster now.

Lucian lifted his rifle. "Stay behind me when we move."

"No."

"Sloane."

"I am not walking into his trap behind you like luggage."

His expression hardened. "That is not what I said."

"It is what you meant."

"I meant stay where I can see you."

The words came out low. Rougher than usual.

For a second, the room seemed too small for the two of them and every terrible thing they had inherited from her forgotten self.

Sloane stepped closer, close enough to see the strain held tight at the corners of his eyes.

"Then keep up," she said.

His gaze dropped to her mouth and returned to her eyes so quickly she might have imagined it.

"Always," Lucian said.

Her phone vibrated a third time.

The message was from Rook.

Sloane read it once.

Then again, because the words refused to become sense.

Rook's message ended with a single line: "Do you remember the eighth contract, Sloane? Bring it, and I'll let your sister live."

Sloane stared at the screen. She had no idea what the eighth contract was.
